result: The computational model qualitatively predicts alterations in swing and stance phase durations during locomotion after hemisection. The model's predictions are compared with experimental data across tied-belt and split-belt conditions, showing overall agreement despite some inconsistencies.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the model's predictive capability. The editor states the study provides 'convincing evidence that this model is capable of qualitatively predicting alterations to the swing and stance phase durations.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the model is able to replicate very well several experimental findings,' providing 'strong validation for the model.' Reviewer 2 states 'the model's predictions match the data, which is good.'

result: Following hemisection, the contralesional (left) side of the spinal network is mostly controlled by supraspinal drives operating in a flexor-driven regime, while the ipsilesional (right) side is mostly controlled by somatosensory feedback operating in a state-machine regime.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly highlights this as a strength, stating 'The study provides insights about interactions between the left and right side of the spinal locomotor networks, and how these interactions depend on the mode of operation, as determined by speed and state of the nervous system.' No reviewer challenges this core mechanistic prediction of the model.

result: Having the ipsilesional hindlimb step on the slow belt during split-belt locomotion substantially reduces the effects of lateral hemisection and produces results similar to the intact state, whereas having it step on the fast belt increases asymmetry between hindlimbs.
evaluation: This finding is not explicitly critiqued by any reviewer. The editor describes the study as providing 'convincing evidence' for predictions about locomotion 'on intact or split-belt treadmills.' Reviewer 1 notes the model 'is able to replicate very well several experimental findings,' which would include these split-belt results presented throughout the manuscript.

result: During tied-belt locomotion after hemisection, the intact contralesional side shows speed-dependent changes similar to intact cats, while the ipsilesional side shows increased flexor (swing) phase durations and decreased extensor (stance) phase durations, particularly a large proportional increase in swing phase duration.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these tied-belt findings. The editor states the modeling and experimental work provide 'convincing evidence' for predictions about 'alterations to the swing and stance phase durations during locomotion at different speeds.' Reviewer 1 emphasizes the model 'is able to replicate very well several experimental findings,' which encompasses these tied-belt results.

result: In contrast to model simulations, experimental data show that stance durations on the right ipsilesional side did not change following hemisection during tied-belt and Left slow/Right fast split-belt locomotion, although swing durations increased as predicted.
evaluation: This discrepancy between model and experiment is acknowledged by the authors and not disputed by reviewers. The editor notes the study provides evidence the model is 'capable of qualitatively predicting' changes, implying acceptance of some quantitative differences. Reviewer 1 states 'My concerns were well addressed by the authors,' suggesting any issues with model-experiment discrepancies were satisfactorily explained.

result: In the Left slow/Right fast split-belt condition, the left contralesional side shows relatively constant cycle and phase durations with increased right belt speed, while the right ipsilesional side shows pronounced speed-dependent reduction of stance and increase of swing durations, with duty factor falling below 50% at higher speeds.
evaluation: These specific split-belt findings are not challenged by reviewers. The editor affirms the study provides 'convincing evidence' for predictions about split-belt locomotion. Reviewer 1 notes the model replicates experimental findings 'very well,' and Reviewer 2 states 'the model's predictions match the data,' which would include these Left slow/Right fast results.

result: In the Left fast/Right slow split-belt condition, cycle and phase durations on both sides show minimal changes with increasing left belt speed, remaining similar to the intact state except for a small increase in swing duration in the ipsilesional hindlimb.
evaluation: Reviewers do not dispute these Left fast/Right slow findings. The editor's statement that the study provides 'convincing evidence' for split-belt predictions encompasses this condition. Reviewer 1's comment that the model 'is able to replicate very well several experimental findings' and Reviewer 2's statement that 'the model's predictions match the data' support these results.

result: The model proposes mechanistic explanations for observed changes: increased ipsilesional swing duration results from greater influence of hip flexor feedback (SF-E1) due to loss of presynaptic inhibition; increased contralesional stance duration may result from increased inhibition via commissural interneurons and greater load-related group Ib feedback (SF-E2).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly praises this aspect, stating 'the putative neural circuit mechanisms that the model uncovers are super cool if they can be tested in an animal.' Reviewer 1 notes the study 'provides insights about interactions between the left and right side of the spinal locomotor networks,' which relates to these mechanistic explanations. No reviewer challenges these proposed mechanisms.

result: The model has limitations including lack of fore-hindlimb interactions, musculoskeletal properties, pattern formation networks, and neuroplastic changes following SCI, which may explain discrepancies between simulated and experimental data.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these limitations without disputing them. The editor describes the model as providing 'qualitatively' (not quantitatively) accurate predictions, implicitly accepting limitations. Reviewer 2 specifically notes 'the discussion points to modeling plasticity after SCI, which will be important,' affirming this as a recognized limitation and future direction.

result: Modeling sensorimotor interactions can be a powerful tool to predict and mechanistically explain changes following incomplete SCI, possibly serving to guide rehabilitation efforts.
evaluation: The editor characterizes the study as 'important' and states it 'will interest neuroscientists studying vertebrate motor systems, including researchers working on motor dysfunction after spinal cord injury.' Reviewer 1 emphasizes the model's 'utility as a tool to investigate the operations of mammalian spinal locomotor networks.' Reviewer 2 calls the findings 'interesting' and the mechanisms 'super cool.'

result: The hemisected model was created by setting all supraspinal drives from the right side to zero in the previously published intact model, without changing any other parameters. The model architecture includes rhythm generators with flexor and extensor half-centers, commissural interneuronal pathways, and sensory feedback components (SF-E1 and SF-E2).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes as a strength that 'Despite only altering the connections in the model, the model is able to replicate very well several experimental findings.' This validates the modeling approach of only removing supraspinal drives without parameter adjustments. No reviewer challenges the model architecture or methodology.
